title: Compromise Infrastructure
summary: Compromise Infrastructure is the acquisition of operational assets by taking over systems that belong to somebody else, rather than buying or renting them. The target set includes physical and cloud servers, domains, network devices, and third-party web or DNS services, and large numbers of low-value machines may be seized to assemble a botnet. The value is twofold: the operator avoids purchase records entirely, and traffic flows to or from hosts with an established reputation, so it resembles normal business communication. Common uses include staging phishing content, relaying traffic through proxies, and positioning on infrastructure near a victim, for example through nearby wireless networks. Unlike Acquire Infrastructure, no payment or registration trail exists; the evidence is on the victim side in the form of unexpected administrative logins, modified configurations, new certificates, and sudden changes in outbound traffic. Defenders separate this from ordinary administration by confirming whether the change was ticketed, who authorised it, and whether timing aligns with a maintenance window.

beginner.definition: This technique is about attackers taking control of computers, servers, or domains that belong to other people. They do not buy anything. They break in and use what is already there. The result is a base for attacks that hides their true identity.
beginner.whyItMatters: Traffic from a hijacked system looks normal, because the system is real and trusted. The owner may keep working and never notice. Victims and investigators may blame the wrong organisation. This is why simply checking whether a destination is reputable is not enough.
howItWorks: The attacker finds a weakly protected server, device, or account that belongs to someone else.
They gain access using stolen credentials, a known flaw, or a guessable password.
They install their tools and quietly change settings so their access survives restarts.
They use the system to send phishing mail, host pages, or relay control traffic.
They hide their activity inside the normal traffic that the system already produces.
They may recruit many such machines at once, or take over networks built by other criminals.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital night desk left unattended for a moment. A stranger sits behind it and answers the phone. Callers hear the correct greeting and share private details. Nothing was bought and nothing was broken, yet the desk is now working for the wrong person.
takeaways: Trusted infrastructure can still be hostile if someone else has taken it over.
Unusual admin logins and setting changes are the clearest early evidence.
Patch levels and password hygiene directly reduce how easily your systems are borrowed.

objectives: Explain what Compromise Infrastructure means and how it differs from Acquire Infrastructure.
Describe the kinds of third-party systems attackers commonly take over.
Identify the log sources that reveal unauthorised configuration changes.
Distinguish malicious use of a host from legitimate administration by its owner.
Describe how asset hardening reduces the chance of being used as a relay.
